title: When a signer's key is lost, verification falls back from cryptography to social and video proof
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.2.2.1 splits address updates by key availability. If the original key is accessible (A.2.11.1.3.2.2.2.1.1), the signer signs a message with it "clearly stat[ing] the intent to replace the existing signer address with the new address" — clean cryptographic continuity, where the old key authorizes its own succession.

If the key is lost (A.2.11.1.3.2.2.2.1.2), "the signer must verify their identity to the remaining signers through alternative verification methods such as: [a]uthentication through a verified social media or publicly associated account; [l]ive verification via video call with existing signers; [o]ther comparable verification methods."

Acknowledging this path is more honest than most key-management policies, which simply assume keys persist. Key loss is common, and without a defined recovery route each occurrence becomes an improvised decision under pressure — the exact conditions social engineering exploits.

But it should be read for what it is: the security of a multisig ultimately rests on the remaining signers' ability to recognize a colleague, not on cryptography. Video calls are increasingly forgeable, and a "publicly associated account" is itself takeover-prone. For a pseudonymous signer whose only prior binding to the multisig was the lost key, there may be little left to verify against.

This is the same shape as the Resilience Fund's attestation fallback, where a verified beneficiary vouches for an applicant with no onchain proof. In both cases the system's last resort is social consensus, and both place that resort at exactly the point where an attacker would prefer to attack.
description: With the original key inaccessible, identity is re-established through a verified social account, a live video call with existing signers, or comparable methods
